title: How to Get Usage Rights for Customer Photos Before You Run Ads
excerpt: Customer photos beat studio shots in paid social, but running them without permission invites takedowns. Ask in the review form and log every consent.
body: Customer photos consistently outperform studio images in paid social, and using them without permission is the fastest way to turn a happy review into a complaint or a takedown request. The fix is not legal boilerplate buried in your terms of service. It is a clear ask written in plain language at the moment someone uploads a photo, plus a record that proves which assets you are allowed to run and where you are allowed to run them.

Make the request part of the review form instead of an afterthought. One sentence next to the upload button saying that submitting a photo lets you feature it in marketing, with credit to the customer handle, gets an informed yes from most contributors. Add a checkbox only if your counsel insists on explicit consent, and keep the wording short enough to read on a phone. Anything longer becomes a wall of text people agree to without reading, which is worse for you than asking nothing at all.

Track consent next to the asset rather than in your inbox. For every photo you intend to use, store the reviewer name or handle, the date permission was given, the product, and the original review text. When an agency or a freelancer assembles ads six months from now, that record tells them precisely what is fair game. A shared folder of downloaded images with no permission trail is how a brand ends up pulling a live campaign mid flight and paying for the media anyway.

Build a respectful way to say no. Some customers are glad to be featured on your site but not in paid ads, or fine with email but not with their face across social platforms. You need a response path: when someone asks you to remove an image, take it out of active campaigns within a day and log the decision so it never gets reused by accident. Treat these requests as routine operations rather than emergencies, and your team will stop viewing consent as an obstacle to shipping work.

Keep the pipeline full so paid usage never becomes a scramble. Ask for photos a few days after delivery, when the product has arrived but the excitement has not faded, and rotate which products you request each month so your library does not fill up with one hero SKU. Tag submissions inside your review tool as soon as they arrive, separating those with photo permission from text only reviews, so you are never guessing during a campaign build.

Finally, give something back. A thank you note, a small credit, or simply tagging the creator when the ad runs turns a one time permission into a relationship that produces more content and sometimes a repeat purchase. The DTCwise Reviews category at /category/reviews keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the Okendo listing at /tool/okendo is a good place to check whether its request flows and media rights handling match the process you want to run.
